notes.1i: Most candidates clearly showed the addition as required and correctly completed the calculation, giving the percentage of the fruit that was made up of sugars. Most candidates gave the answer to no more than two decimal places.
notes.1ii: Most candidates used the headings given in the table to correctly label the x-axis and the y-axis. Some candidates, however, labelled the incorrect axis or gave incomplete headings. The stronger candidates used a scale of 2 to 2cm for the y-axis. Many candidates plotted the horizontal line at the top of each bar precisely and with a thin line. The most common errors were not including a full axis label for each axis, omitting the units for the y-axis, not labelling the scale every 2cm and drawing lines which were too thick.
notes.1iii: Many candidates correctly named a source of sucrose in the plant as the leaves and named the process used for loading the sucrose into the phloem tissue as active transport.
notes.1iv: The stronger candidates used a scale of 1 to 2cm for the x-axis, labelling the scale every 2cm. Some candidates selected a suitable scale for the y-axis so that the results recorded in Question 1(a)
notes.1v: Many candidates were able to use the graph and the time stated in Question 1(a)
notes.1vi: The stronger candidates identified one significant source of error as the difficulty of identifying the appearance of the first colour change.
notes.1vii: Many candidates correctly suggested that increasing the number of sucrose concentrations below 2.0% would improve the procedure to obtain a more accurate estimate of the percentage concentration of sucrose solution in the fruit extract. The stronger candidates stated that at least five concentrations below 2.0% should be used and the difference between the concentrations should be as small as possible.
notes.2i: Credit was awarded to candidates whose drawings did not include any shading and used most of the space provided. The stronger candidates gained credit for carefully following the instructions and drawing the epidermis and the vascular bundles in the stem. Many candidates gained credit for drawing one outer vascular bundle and three inner vascular bundles. Credit was also given to those candidates who showed subdivision of the vascular bundles and used a ruled label line and label to identify the cortex.
notes.2ii: The majority of candidates used the eyepiece graticule in the microscope to measure the total length of the four cells (L) and the depth of one of the cells (D) and recorded the number of eyepiece graticule units as whole numbers.
notes.2iii: Credit was awarded to candidates whose drawings were made using a sharp pencil to produce lines which were continuous and used most of the space provided. Many candidates were able to draw four cells from around the air spaces. Many candidates were credited for showing each cell touching at least one of the other cells. Credit was also given to those candidates who drew the correct shape for these cells. Most candidates used a ruled label line and label to identify the cell wall of one cell.
notes.2iv: Many candidates correctly suggested that K1 might grow in an aquatic habitat.
notes.2b: Many candidates correctly measured the width of the stem as shown by the line X–Y. To calculate the actual width of the stem the stronger candidates showed the multiplication of the number of eyepiece graticule units by 29.5. Most candidates gave the answer to no more than two decimal places with the appropriate units (µm). The most common errors were to omit the units and not show all of the steps in the calculation.
notes.2c: The stronger candidates used label lines to show three features in Fig. 2.3 and described next to each line how each feature was different from the specimen on K1. Many candidates stated three observable differences between Fig. 2.3 and K1, e.g. K1 had vascular bundles touching while in Fig. 2.3 the vascular bundles were separated from each other.
notes.key_messages: Key events occurring in the immune response are the recognition by the immune system cells of the non-self (foreign) antigen and activation of specific lymphocytes. Some questions that are set for Topic 11, Immunity, are based on unfamiliar material and do not always identify the antigen for the candidate. When responding to questions such as this, a good introduction would be to identify the non-self antigen.
